Secondly, how can I also estimate the QTL interval size (bp) with R/qtl?

Thanks!

>  Is there a function in R/qtl that will give me the positions of the flanking markers of the QTL-interval in my genetic map - so that I can say the QTL interval is from position x to position y and then check the genes within that region?.

Use lodint() or bayesint() to get the QTL interval; use the argument expandtomarkers=TRUE to have the end points of the interval be at markers.

>
> Secondly, how can I also estimate the QTL interval size (bp) with R/qtl?

These functions use whatever map distances you've provided. The function interpPositions() can help to interpolate between a genetic and physical map, or use replacemap().

karl

messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] treatment of sex column with perm.Xsp=TRUE
messages.body_plain:
The sex phenotype column is needed for qtl analysis on the X chromosome, whether you're doing a permutation test or not, and whether perm.Xsp=TRUE or =FALSE.

The method of permutations is the same whether perm.Xsp=TRUE or =FALSE, and is not done stratified by sex. For the X chromosome in a backcross or intercross, males and females each have a single recombinant X chromosome, and we're effectively shuffling those across all individuals.

karl

messages.body_plain:
If you're using sex as a phenotype, you wouldn't want to also include it as a covariate.

And you can't really deal with X chromosome data properly in this case. Our handling of the X chromosome presumes that the genetic causes of sex are understood (XX = female, XY = male), in which case sex as an outcome doesn't make much sense.

messages.body_plain:
> I have a dataset (SSD lines, GBS data) for which I already know the linkage groups and the order of the markers. I'd like to use R/qtl just to compute the maps of the linkage groups. Also, the dataset has some missing datapoints so this is why I want to use R/qtl, to calculate multipoint estimates of the recombination fractions.
>
> How do I tell R/qtl to take the known orders from a file (or from a command line), then calculate the map for each linkage group, then returning the map to a file?

If you create a CSV file with the genotypes, with markers as columns and lines as rows, use the 2nd row to indicate the linkage group identifiers. When imported into R with the read.cross() function, the order of the markers in the file is used as the order of markers along each linkage group. Arbitrary locations are assigned, or you can use a third row to give your own initial estimates of positions.

Then use est.map to estimate the inter-marker distances; it takes the marker order as truth.

> Do I need to use the argmax function prior to est.map, or does R/qtl calculates true multipoint on non-imputed data?

Don't try to impute missing data. R/qtl uses a hidden Markov model to derive multipoint estimates and can deal with the missing data.

karl

messages.subject_clean: dropping markers with a defined RF
messages.body_plain:
Hi SKY - you have two options.
1) If your are able to estimate your genetic map, the best approach is to use: pickMarkerSubset. This lets you weight markers by missing data etc. and choose the best ones in a given interval. For example, if you set

min.distance = 2, you will only retain the best marker in every 2cM window. It is a bit tricky to use though. There is also qtlTools:repPickMarkerSubset which makes it a bit more user friendly. For example:

> culled.cross = repPickMarkerSubset(orig.cross, min.distance = 2) # creates a new cross object with only a single marker in every 2 cM window.

2) Alternatively, if your genotype matrix is too big to estimate a map (>~10k markers), you can cull by the recombination fractions chromosome-by-chromosome using qtlTools::dropSimilarMarkers. This employs the protocol you describe above - find and cull markers that have low recombination fractions. You can define your recombination fraction threshold via the rf.threshold argument. However, this approach does not perform quite as well as scanning across the map via pickMarkerSubset since it is agnostic to the order of markers.
Good luck,
John

I prefer the penalized LOD score criterion, discussed in chapter 9 of the R/qtl book (http://rqtl.org/book); also see:

  Broman KW, Speed TP (2002) A model selection approach for the identification of quantitative trait loci in experimental crosses. J Roy Stat Soc B 64:641-656

  Manichaikul A, Moon JY, Sen Ś, Yandell BS, Broman KW (2009) A model selection approach for the identification of quantitative trait loci in experimental crosses, allowing epistasis. Genetics 181:1077-1086

>  2 :
>  The other question is on the ‘maximal’ number of terms that can be included in the model.
>  I have cases with more than twenty terms (containing QTLs, covariates and different interactions). There is no bug and all terms I have selected are significant according to the Pvalues of the drop one QTL at a time ANOVA TABLE.
> However I have only 300 phenotypic values, and I feel uncomfortable of adding to the formula that much terms, I feel that it should have a statistical power problem for the establishments of the model.
>
> So my question : does the fitqtl function is OK with a ‘high’ number of terms in the formula and is there any indicator to know what is the ‘limit’

It's hard to place a hard limit, but it seems unlikely that you could identify such a complex model with a sample size of 300. I would ignore the pointwise p-values from fitqtl and focus on the LOD scores and compare them to the permutation-based thresholds that adjust for the search across the genome.

karl
